text: Two acronyms, three letters each, describing the exact same three jobs — getting data out of a source, changing its shape, and putting it somewhere useful. The only real difference between them is the order those three jobs happen in, and that order changes more than you'd expect.

ETL stands for Extract, Transform, Load. Data gets pulled from the source, transformed in a separate processing engine sitting in between, and only then loaded into the destination, already in its final, clean shape. Every downstream consumer only ever sees data that's already been cleaned.

ELT flips the last two steps: Extract, Load, Transform. Data gets pulled from the source and loaded into the destination essentially as-is, raw and unclean, and the actual transformation happens afterward, inside the destination system itself — a cloud warehouse like Azure Synapse Analytics, for example.

Data Factory supports both patterns, but in modern cloud architecture its pipelines lean ELT-first in practice. A Copy activity moves raw data into a centralized lake or warehouse first, and the real transformation happens afterward — either with Data Factory's own mapping data flows, or by calling out to a dedicated engine like Synapse or Databricks.

Two real things changed to make ELT the modern default. Storage got cheap enough that keeping a full copy of raw data around stopped being a real cost concern. And cloud warehouses got powerful enough to transform enormous datasets faster than a dedicated ETL engine ever could on its own.
